title: Write a Safe Bash Backup Script
intro: The Linux tutorials were all one-liners. Real automation means scripts — and a script that keeps going after an error, or mangles a path with a space in it, can do real damage. Write one defensively.

steps.prompt: Write backup.sh: (1) shebang #!/usr/bin/env bash; (2) 'set -euo pipefail'; (3) if the number of arguments ($#) isn't exactly 1, print a usage message to stderr (>&2) and 'exit 1'; (4) store the argument in a quoted variable (src="$1"); (5) create a tar.gz in /backups named after the directory plus today's date (date +%F), with 'tar -czf', quoting every variable.
steps.hint: Structure: shebang → set -euo pipefail → argument check (if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then echo "usage: $0 <dir>" >&2; exit 1; fi) → src="$1" → build the destination path with $(basename "$src") and $(date +%F) → tar -czf "$dest" "$src".
steps.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
  echo "usage: $0 <directory>" >&2
  exit 1
fi

src="$1"
dest="/backups/$(basename "$src")-$(date +%F).tar.gz"

tar -czf "$dest" "$src"
echo "backup written to $dest"
steps.explanation: Fails fast on bad input or any failed command, and handles paths with spaces correctly.
steps.why: 'set -e' stops at the first failing command (without it, a failed tar still prints 'backup written' — the silent-success pattern behind linux-incident-005's two weeks of missing backups). '-u' turns a typo'd variable into an error instead of an empty string, '-o pipefail' makes a pipeline fail if ANY command in it fails. Quoting every "$var" keeps a path like '/data/my files' as one argument instead of two. Errors go to stderr (>&2) so cron logs and callers can tell them apart from normal output.
